title: OIDC username claim trusted as local-account key -> account takeover
rationale: Root cause is oidc_authentication.py:82-86: after JWT validation the username claim is the sole key into get_user_by_username, and any matched account is returned as authenticated. _check_user_change (lines 160-165) then converts a matched local account into an OIDC account (is_oidc_user=True, set_unusable_password), so an attacker who controls the configured OIDC_USERNAME claim can assert an existing local user's name and take over that account. The fix enforces, at the sink, that a username-claim match against a pre-existing non-OIDC account (is_oidc_user is False) is rejected before any state change or session is granted. Legitimate OIDC users carry is_oidc_user=True (set at creation, line 115), so they are unaffected; brand-new OIDC users go through _create_user, also unaffected. This stops local-account takeover. Full (iss, sub) immutable-claim binding as the long-term recommendation requires a schema/model change (a new sub field) that exceeds a minimal root-cause fix; this change closes the takeover primitive with no migration.
variants_checked: oidc_authentication.py:_validate_jwt (the cited sink, fixed); oidc_authentication.py:_create_user line 136 (second get_user_by_username call — only reached on IntegrityError after a fresh OIDC create, returns a user that was just created as is_oidc_user=True, not a takeover vector); jwt_authentication.py:_validate_jwt line 73 (uses get_user_by_username but the token is SecObserve's own JWT signed with JWT_Secret, not an external IdP claim — different trust model, not the OIDC mutable-claim issue, so intentionally not changed); core/services/product_api_token.py:17 (internal product-token user lookup, not an auth-claim path).
bypass_considered: Considered an attacker who, instead of matching an existing local admin name, registers via OIDC first so the account is created with is_oidc_user=True, then relies on a mutable claim to later collide with that same OIDC username. The check still gates on is_oidc_user, so this does not reach the local-account takeover state. The remaining residual is OIDC-user-vs-OIDC-user collision when OIDC_USERNAME maps to a non-unique/self-serviceable claim (two distinct IdP identities asserting the same username value) — that is the (iss, sub) binding gap and is documented as out of scope for this minimal diff because it needs a sub-storage schema change; it is not a local-account takeover, which is the finding's exploit.
test_note:
Added test_validate_jwt_user_found_local_account to backend/unittests/access_control/services/test_oidc_authentication.py (mirrors test_validate_jwt_user_found but the matched user has is_oidc_user=False, asserting AuthenticationFailed is raised and _check_user_change is never called). It fails before the change (user is returned/linked) and passes after. Diff for the test below:

     @patch("application.access_control.services.oidc_authentication.get_user_by_username")

+        self,

+        jwt_mock.return_value = {"preferred_username": local_user.username}

     @patch("application.access_control.services.oidc_authentication.decode")

review_reason: The single hunk inserts an `is_oidc_user` gate at oidc_authentication.py:83, immediately after `get_user_by_username` and before `_check_user_change`, which is the correct chokepoint on the path to line 79. It fixes the root cause: `_check_user_change` (lines 160-162) silently flips a matched local account's `is_oidc_user` to True, enabling OIDC-token-to-local-account takeover (including superusers); the patch rejects that collision with `AuthenticationFailed` instead of mutating the account. No new input is trusted (`is_oidc_user` is a server-side DB field), no validation is weakened, and the raised exception matches the surrounding error-handling style.
